entry.title: Upside Down Art
entry.content:
Book

“Tilda Tries Again” written and illustrated by Tom Percival

Response Art

After reading this book, I ask the group to create a topsy-turvy image. I include questions such as ‘what does topsy-turvy feel like?’ and ‘or does this feeling have a color or shape to it?

Process Questions

  1. What things or situations in life make you feel topsy-turvy?
  2. What are some coping skills or strategies you’ve learned that help you when you’re feeling this way?

Therapeutic Benefits

The book focuses on themes related to resiliency, acceptance, and developing coping skills when going through change or life transitions. Topsy-turvy changes could include a new diagnosis, being relocated to a new home, having your plans fall through, or even conflict in relationships. The art process following the reading assists in externalizing the topsy-turvy feeling as it becomes embodied through shape and color. The process increases self-awareness, building resilience and providing validation of felt emotions.

Materials

  • Construction paper
  • Color pens and markers
  • Color pencils
  • Large tempera sticks
entry.summary: Coping skills when things go topsy-turvy

entry.title: Shaping My Heart
entry.content:
Book

The Heart and the Bottle written and illustrated Oliver Jeffers

Response Art

Mold air dry clay into the shape of a heart. Add tile pieces or other miscellaneous items to reflect how your heart has changed over the years. Paint your heart or add color if desired. If you don’t have clay, use paper and coloring utensils to draw a heart instead.

Process Questions

  1. What inspired the choice of colors and designs of your heart?
  2. Does the color or design reflect your life experiences at all? If so, how?

Therapeutic Benefits

The book helps provide language for navigating grief and loss. It is a gentle reminder that overprotecting our heart from enduring more hardship can stump curiosity, inner growth, and keep us from fully living as exemplified by the main character. The story validates all the complex feelings that come with grief and loss, and encourages supportive communities to come alongside those who’re grieving. The art portion gives participants the opportunity to share about their own life experiences and find acceptance in moving forward while still acknowledging what was lost.

Materials

  • DAS non-toxic air drying modeling clay (I like the white version)
  • Tile or ceramic pieces
  • Beads
  • Paint if desired
  • Coloring pens
  • Paper
entry.summary: A book that addresses grief, loss, and a broken heart

entry.title: “Say Something!” by Peter H. Reynolds
entry.content:
Book

“Letters to Live By: An Alphabet Book with Intention” Written by Lisa Frenkel Riddiough and Illustrated by Asa Gilland

Response Art

After reading this book, I instruct the group to pick a value or intention that begins with the first letter of their name. Then, to write that value in a big font across their paper. Add colors, shapes, and pictures to reflect the value. If a participant would like to write intentions using all the letters in their name, they can!

Process Questions

  1. What intention or personal value is most important to you? How do the colors, shapes, or pictures you drew support this?
  2. What gets in the way of you living out this value?

Therapeutic Benefits

This book is simple yet intentionally written to help readers examine their own personal values and intentions for living. The playful and whimsical illustrations that reflect each value portrayed in the book can inspire group participants to think of their own through colors and illustrations. The art project is a strengths-based approach, deriving from positive psychology, and can increase self-awareness, promote higher self-esteem, and help foster actionable steps in line with one’s own personal values.

Materials

  • Paper
  • Coloring pens
  • Color pencils
entry.summary: Getting in touch with your personal values and what matters most

entry.title: Empowering Word Collage
entry.content:
Book

The book we featured this week in my senior community was “Say Something!” by Peter H. Reynolds. It’s a great read focused around speaking up, using your voice and other nonverbal forms of self-expression. The book can increase self-esteem while promoting individuality and a sense of agency.

Response Art

The art process includes exploring a mixed variety of cut-out words (if you need ideas of words, pick some from the book!) to rearrange and create a phrase or word you want to tell the world or your community. Glue the word or phrase to the center of your paper and make art around it. What additional images, patterns, or colors come to mind when you read this word or phrase? Think of this like protest art!

Process Questions

  1. What word or phrase did you come up with? How does this word or phrase show up in your life or community?
  2. Did you add any drawings or colors around the word or phrase?

Therapeutic Benefits

The overall process of creating a word collage for yourself or community can shape personal values and build confidence. The book and the art fosters self-awareness and independence, increasing a sense of control for those who feel like their voice is lost, ignored, or forgotten.

Materials

  • 8.5” x 11” white printer paper, drawing paper or cardstock (feel free to go bigger or smaller)
  • Pre-cut out words
  • Glue
  • Scissors
  • Coloring pencils/pens, pencil and eraser
  • Oil pastels
  • Alphabet letter foam stickers

entry.title: “Henry’s Freedom Box” by Ellen Levine and Kadir Nelson

link.title: “Henry’s Freedom Box” by Ellen Levine and Kadir Nelson

entry.content:
Book

“Henry’s Freedom Box” by Ellen Levine and Kadir Nelson addresses resilience, injustice, and the fight for freedom. It’s a great choice for leading a group conversation around personal values, sacrifice, and perseverance.

Response Art

The art process includes drawing a symbol of freedom at the center of a 5.5” x8.5” paper (cut a standard printing paper in half or use the full size). I pre-made same sized pages with a bird at the center representing freedom for them to color into. Birds in the book symbolize freedom and hope. Then, fold the paper with the drawing on the inside into a paper box. See this tutorial to learn how to fold your paper easily into a box. Add words or decorations on the outside of your origami freedom box if desired.

Process Questions

  1. What image of freedom came up for you? How do your colors or drawing reflect this?
  2. Did you add anything else around the outside of your freedom box? What was it like making your drawing into a physical box?

Therapeutic Benefits

The overall process promotes meaning-making in the art through symbolic and representational thought. It fosters autonomy, a sense of resiliency, and emotional expression, while also getting in touch with personal values.

Materials

  • 5.5” x 8.5” white printer paper or cardstock
  • Coloring pencils/pens, pencil and eraser
  • Decorative stickers
  • Glitter
entry.summary: A conversation on personal values, sacrifice, and perseverance

entry.title: “After the Fall: How Humpty Dumpty Got Back Up Again” by Dan Santat

link.title: “After the Fall: How Humpty Dumpty Got Back Up Again” by Dan Santat

entry.content:
Book

The book featured in my art groups this week was “After the Fall: How Humpty Dumpty Got Back Up Again” by Dan Santat. It is a perfect read for leading an art discussion on fears, confidence, and bravery.

Response Art

The art process includes drawing or coloring in a brick wall that represents a fear or a personal problem while thinking about the walls’ height in relation to your experience of the problem. For my older adults, I found preprinting coloring pages of brick walls to color on was the best approach. Then, I folded the paper into a paper plane to represent our ability to reach past fears or problems. If you want, add personal self-affirmations onto the paper plane. Throwing the paper plane after discussing these barriers becomes a cathartic way for releasing the frustrations. And it’s fun to race the paper planes!

Process Questions

  1. How did it feel when you made your brick wall into a paper airplane?
  2. What does the process show you about letting go and releasing fears, or reaching past your problems?
  3. Any encouraging words to tell ‘your wall’?

Therapeutic Benefits

The artwork evokes conversation around perseverance through trials, resulting in a collective understanding of human struggle and resiliency. The overall process promotes a sense of agency, building self-esteem, problem solving, and positive thinking.

Materials

Coloring paper, coloring pencils/pens, pencil and eraser
entry.summary: A perfect read for leading an art discussion on fears, confidence, and bravery

entry.title: “Martin Rising” by Andrea Davis Pinkney & Brian Pinkney

link.title: “Martin Rising” by Andrea Davis Pinkney & Brian Pinkney

entry.content:
Book

This week, I used the book “Martin Rising” by Andrea Davis Pinkney & Brian Pinkney. We reflected on community, connection, and unity through art.

Response Art

The process includes reading a select few poems from the book, discussing the themes, and tracing our hands or coloring paper in the shape of a hand to personalize with words or images. Participants were asked to add imagery or words that help them explore the content deeper, and to apply the content to their own lives if desired. Questions like ‘What change do you want to see in your own communities?’ ‘In yourself?’ and ‘How can we build a better future together?’ The hands were then all put together on a larger piece of butcher paper, with the fingers touching, to reflect community, unity, and inclusion.

Process Questions

  1. What was it like to trace your hand and add your own images or words representing community and change?
  2. How was it intercrossing each other’s hands onto the larger piece of paper? What feelings came up for you?

Therapeutic Benefits

The artwork evokes conversation around our own personal values and need for action. The overall process promotes a sense of agency and independence, increasing interpersonal skills and self-awareness.

Materials

Skintone craft paper, coloring pencils/pens, gem stickers, gluestick, scissors, pencil
entry.summary: A book that explores community, connection, and finding a sense of unity
